{{real world}} {{sidebar actor |name = Michael Pataki |image = Karnas.jpg |caption = ...as Karnas |image2 = Korax, 2268.jpg |caption2 = ...as Korax |birth name = Michael Pataki |birthday = {{d|16|January|1938}} |birthplace = Youngstown, Ohio, USA |deathday = {{d|15|April|2010}} |deathplace = North Hollywood, California, USA |roles = Actor |characters = [[Korax]];
[[Karnas]] }} '''Michael Pataki''' {{born|16|January|1938|died|15|April|2010}} was an actor who played [[Korax]] in the {{s|TOS}} [[TOS Season 2|second season]] episode {{e|The Trouble with Tribbles}} and [[Karnas]] in the {{s|TNG}} [[TNG Season 1|first season]] episode {{e|Too Short A Season}}. Archive footage of his role in "The Trouble with Tribbles" was used in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 5|fifth season]] episode {{e|Trials and Tribble-ations}}. == Early life and career == Pataki was [[Star Trek birthdays#January|born]] in Youngstown, Ohio, to Hungarian parents. He was a graduate of the University of Southern California, where he majored in drama and political science. Pataki had a career in film and on television which spanned over five decades. He made his debut with an uncredited role in {{wt|The Young Lions (film)|The Young Lions}} (1958, starring [[Marlon Brando]], featuring [[Parley Baer]], [[Hal Baylor]], [[Paul Comi]] and [[Robert Ellenstein]]). Later that year, he made his first television appearance in an episode of ''M Squad'', working with fellow ''Next Generation'' alum [[Bill Erwin]]. Throughout the 1960s, Pataki acted predominantly on television, appearing on such series as ''[[The Twilight Zone]]'' (1961, starring ''Original Series'' actor [[Leonard Nimoy]] and {{s|ENT}} guest actor [[Dean Stockwell]]), {{wt|Rawhide (TV series)|Rawhide}} (with Paul Comi and [[John McLiam]]), {{wt|My Favorite Martian}} (starring [[Ray Walston]]), {{wt|Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea (TV series)|Voyage to the Bottom}} (with [[Arch Whiting]] and [[Jason Wingreen]]), and ''[[Mission: Impossible]]''. Pataki also appeared in multiple episodes of {{wt|The Flying Nun}}, playing three different characters over the show's three seasons. Among those he worked with on this series were ''Original Series'' actresses [[Susan Howard]], [[Sandra Smith]], [[Tania Lemani]], and [[Louise Sorel]]. Pataki also appeared in two 1966 "King Tut" episodes of {{wt|Batman (TV series)|Batman}}, both co-starring [[Sid Haig]] and [[Marianna Hill]]. In 1969, Pataki appeared in his first feature film since the 1950s, playing one of the mimes in {{wt|Easy Rider}}. ''Original Series'' guest performers [[Sabrina Scharf]] and [[Robert Walker]] also had roles in this film. In the same year he appeared as the villainous J.C. in {{wt|The Sidehackers}}, which also included ''Original Series'' guest actor [[Richard Merrifield]] and ''Next Generation'' actor/stuntman [[Erik Cord]]. == Career during the 1970s and 1980s == Pataki and fellow ''Original Series'' guest actors [[Stewart Moss]] and [[Paul Carr]] frequently worked in films and made-for-TV movies from director {{w|Jerry Jameson}}. These productions included {{wt|Brute Corps}} (1972, with [[Charles Macaulay]]), {{wt|The Dirt Gang}} (1972, with [[Michael Forest]]), {{wt|The Bat People}} (1974), {{wt|Airport '77}} (1977, with [[Robert Foxworth]] and [[Robert Hooks]]), and ''Raise the Titanic'' (1980, also with [[Mark L. Taylor]] and [[Michael Ensign]]). Pataki alone appeared in Jameson's TV movies ''The Call of the Wild'' (1976, with [[John McLiam]]), {{wt|Superdome (film)|Superdome}} (1978, with [[Jane Wyatt]]), and ''The Cowboy and the Ballerina'' (1984, with [[Antoinette Bower]] and [[Christopher Lloyd]]). In 1971, Pataki appeared in the B-movie ''The Return of Count Yorga''. That same year, he also appeared in {{wt|The Andromeda Strain (film)|The Andromeda Strain}}, directed by [[Robert Wise]], who went on to direct {{film|1}}. Both of these films featured performers from the ''Original Series'' episode {{e|All Our Yesterdays}}: [[Mariette Hartley]] appeared in the former, [[Kermit Murdock]] in the latter. ([[Bart La Rue]] and [[Garry Walberg]] also appeared in ''The Andromeda Strain''.) The following year, Pataki appeared in an episode of {{wt|Bonanza}}; a year later, he appeared on ''All in the Family'' (and would do so again in 1977), as well as {{wt|Cannon (TV series)|Cannon}} with [[Stewart Moss]] and Arch Whiting and on {{wt|Shaft (TV series)|Shaft}} with [[Michael Ansara]] and [[Ron Soble]]. Pataki and ''Original Series'' guest actress Marianna Hill, having previously worked together on two episodes of ''Batman'', reunited for {{wt|The Baby (film)|The Baby}} (1974) and {{wt|The Last Porno Flick}} (1974). Also in 1974, Pataki appeared in the TV movie ''Indict and Conflict'' with [[William Shatner]]. Pataki later co-starred with Shatner in {{wt|Disaster on the Coastliner}} (1979) and in a 1982 episode of {{wt|T. J. Hooker}}, with [[Jonathan Banks]], [[James Darren]], and [[Richard Herd]]. In 1974, Pataki also made the first of three appearances on {{wt|McCloud (TV series)|McCloud}}, on which [[Ken Lynch]] was a regular. His first episode also featured [[Terri Garr]], [[Eugene Roche]], and [[Gregory Sierra]]. When he next appeared on the program in February 1976, [[Diana Muldaur]] had become a regular. Pataki and Muldaur were also seen in an episode of ''Ellery Queen'', which aired earlier that month. Pataki's third episode of ''McCloud'' also featured [[Vince Howard]]. Pataki and Muldaur would later appear together in the 1982 ''Fitz and Bones'' TV movie ''Terror at Alcatraz'', along with [[Roger C. Carmel]], [[Elisha Cook]], and [[Marc Lawrence]]. In 1975, Pataki played the lead in {{wt|Carnal Madness}} (1975). Two years later, he began playing one of his more well-known roles, as Captain Barbera in the 1977 TV movie ''The Amazing Spider-Man''. This movie spawned a made-for-TV sequel called ''Spider-Man Strikes Back'' the following year, for which Pataki returned, and led to a short-lived cult TV series later in 1978. Pataki played Captain Barbera through both seasons of ''The Amazing Spider-Man'', which aired from 1978 through 1979. Pataki is well-remembered for his role as Count Mallachi in a three-part episode of the sitcom ''Happy Days'' in 1976. Cult movie fans will also remember him for playing Count Dracula in {{wt|Dracula's Dog}} (1978, co-starring [[Jan Shutan]]). Also in 1978, Pataki appeared in the TV movie ''When Every Day Was the Fourth of July'', which featuring his ''The Flying Nun'' co-star (and ''Trek'' alum) Louise Sorel as well as [[Michael Durrell]], [[Bruce French]], and [[Harris Yulin]]. Pataki was one of the many ''Trek'' performers to appear in {{wt|The Onion Field (film)|The Onion Field}} (1979). Among his co-stars in this film were [[John Savage]], [[Ronnie Cox]], Christopher Lloyd, Richard Herd (who also appeared with Pataki in TV's ''Marciano'' that same year), [[K Callan]], [[Phillip Richard Allen]], and [[John de Lancie]]. He also appeared in {{wt|Love at First Bite}} with Robert Ellenstein that same year. Pataki's career showed no sign of stopping by the time the 1980s arrived. In addition to appearances in such hit TV series as {{wt|Charlie's Angels}}, {{wt|WKRP in Cincinati}} (with [[Sam Anderson]] and Robert Hooks), {{wt|Laverne & Shirley}} (with [[David L. Lander]] and [[Michael McKean]]), {{wt|The Jeffersons}}, {{wt|Scarecrow and Mrs. King}} (1985 & 1986, starring [[Kate Jackson]], former with [[Stephen Macht]]), {{wt|Cagney & Lacey}} (with [[Janet MacLachlan]] and [[Natalia Nogulich]]), and {{wt|St. Elsewhere}} (1987, starring [[William Daniels]], [[Ed Begley, Jr.]], Ronnie Cox, [[Christina Pickles]], [[Norman Lloyd]], [[France Nuyen]], [[Bruce Greenwood]] and [[Jennifer Savidge]], with {{s|VOY}} regular [[Robert Picardo]]), he also appeared in such major feature films as {{wt|Dead & Buried}} (1981, with [[Ed Bakey]], [[Glenn Morshower]], and [[Bill Quinn]]), {{wt|Remo Williams: The Adventure Begins}} (1985, with ''Voyager'' star [[Kate Mulgrew]] as well as [[George Coe]], [[Patrick Kilpatrick]] and [[Jeff Allin]]), {{wt|Rocky IV}} (1985, edited by [[John W. Wheeler]]), and {{wt|Halloween 4: The Return of Michael Myers}} (1988, music by [[Alan Howarth]]). In addition, Pataki made numerous appearances on {{wt|The Fall Guy}}, co-starring with [[Gary Lockwood]]. He and Lockwood also appeared in a 1988 episode of ''The Highwayman'', which was a series starring a pre-''Voyager'' [[Tim Russ]]. == Later career and death == By the 1990s, the majority of Pataki's work became voice-over roles on such animated shows as {{wt|Batman: The Animated Series}} (1992), {{wt|The Ren & Stimpy Show}}, and ''Dexter's Laboratory''. In the 2000s, he made on-screen appearances in a few low-budget independent films, including 2003's ''Edge of Nowhere''. In 2010, he appeared in a film called ''Trim'', which also featured '' Voyager'' regular [[Ethan Phillips]]. Pataki [[Star Trek deaths#April|died]] in North Hollywood, California, on 15 April 2010. He was 72 years old. {{el|variety.com/article/VR1118018051.html?categoryid{{=}}1043&cs{{=}}1}} == Other ''Trek'' connections == *''Letter to Loretta'' episode "Vengeance Is Thine" (1959) with [[Clegg Hoyt]] *{{wt|Ripcord (TV series)|Ripcord}} (1961, with Paul Comi) *Three episodes in {{wt|The Lieutenant}} (1963-64) created by [[Gene Roddenberry]] *{{wt|Bob Hope Presents the Chrysler Theatre}} (1964, with [[Sally Kellerman]]) *{{wt|Slattery's People}} (1965, with [[Whit Bissell]] and [[Don Keefer]]) *{{wt|Ben Casey}} (1965, with [[Bill Mumy]]) *''Dream No Evil'' (1970 film) with [[Marc Lawrence]] *{{wt|Dan August}} (1971) with Stewart Moss *''They Call It Murder'' (1971 TV movie) with [[Victor Tayback]] *{{wt|Search (American TV series)|Search}} (1973) with [[Keith Andes]] *''A Man for Hanging'' (1973 TV movie) with [[Brooke Bundy]], Paul Carr, and [[Walker Edmiston]] *{{wt|Kung Fu (1972 TV series)|Kung Fu}} (1974, with [[Keye Luke]]) *''Amy Prentiss'' episode "The Desperate World of Jane Doe" (1974) with [[Andrew Prine]] *{{wt|Harry O}} (1976, with [[Anthony Zerbe]]) *''Benny and Barney: Las Vegas Undercover'' (1977 TV movie) with [[Ted Cassidy]] **{{wt|The Hardy Boys/Nancy Drew Mysteries}} (1977, with [[Marc Alaimo]]) *''Airport '77'' (1977) with [[Monte Markham]] *{{wt|Barney Miller}} (1978, with [[Ron Glass]] and [[James Gregory]]) *''Ruby and Oswald'' (1978) with Bruce French *{{wt|Alice (American TV series)|Alice}} (1978, starring Vic Tayback) *''The Pirate'' (1978 TV movie) with [[Jeff Corey]] *''The White Shadow'' episode "Little Orphan Abner" (1979) with [[Joan Pringle]] *''Samurai'' (1979 TV movie; {{real world}} {{Sidebar actor |name = Matt Malloy |image = Grish.jpg |caption = ...as Grish |birth name = Matthew Malloy |birthday = {{d|12|January|1963}} |birthplace = Hamilton, New York, USA |deathday = |deathplace = |roles = [[:Category:ENT performers|Guest Actor]]; [[:Category:Video game performers|Voice Actor]] |characters = [[Grish]]
[[Omag|Omag (voice)]] }} '''Matt Malloy''' {{born|12|January|1963}} portrayed [[Grish]] in the {{s|ENT}} [[ENT Season 1|first season]] episode {{e|Acquisition}}. He also provided the voice of [[Omag]] in the {{y|2003}} {{video game}} ''[[Star Trek: Elite Force II]]''. == 1990s work == Malloy has been acting since the late 1980s, but it was not until he performed in the 1992 drama ''Wind'' did Malloy work with another ''Trek'' actor, [[Ned Vaughn]]. Malloy has also appeared in {{wt|Mrs. Parker & the Vicious Circle}} (1994, with [[Wallace Shawn]]). ''Hand Gun'' (1994, with [[Seymour Cassel]]), ''Bloodhounds'' (1996, starring [[Corbin Bernsen]] with [[Michael Buchman Silver]]), {{wt|Boys (1996 film)|Boys}} (1996, with [[Christopher Pettiet]] and [[Winona Ryder]]), {{wt|The Alarmist}} (1997, with [[Dennis Cockrum]]). {{wt|As Good as It Gets}} (1997, with [[Kaitlin Hopkins]]), {{wt|Starstruck (1998 film)|Starstruck}} (1998, with [[Spencer Garrett]]), {{wt|Armageddon (1998 film)|Armageddon}} (1998, co-written by [[J.J. Abrams]], with [[Jeff Austin]], [[Brian Brophy]], [[Jason Isaacs]], [[Jim Fitzpatrick]], [[Googy Gress]], [[Anthony Guidera]], [[James Harper]], [[John Mahon]], [[J. Patrick McCormack]], [[Andy Milder]] and [[Lawrence Tierney]]), {{wt|Playing by Heart}} (1998, starring [[Gillian Anderson]] and [[Sean Connery]], with Michael Buchman Silver, [[David Clennon]], [[April Grace]], [[Tim Halligan]] and [[Kellie Waymire]]) and {{wt|Election (1999 film)|Election}} (1999, with [[Molly Hagan]], [[Mark Harelik]] and [[Holmes R. Osborne]]). == 2000s work == In 2000, Malloy appeared in {{wt|Drop Dead Gorgeous (film)|Drop Dead Gorgeous}} (with [[Kirstie Alley]] and ''Next Generation'' guest [[Kirsten Dunst]]). In the 21st century, Malloy in {{wt|Everything Put Together}} (2000, with [[Shelly Desai]], [[Tom McCleister]] and [[Alan Ruck]]), {{wt|South of Heaven, West of Hell}} (2000, with [[Noble Willingham]]), {{wt|Perfect Murder, Perfect Town}} (2000, with [[Ronny Cox]], [[James G. MacDonald]], [[John Rubinstein]] and [[Sean Whalen]]), {{wt|Finding Forrester}} (2000, with [[F. Murray Abraham]], April Grace and [[Michael Nouri]]), {{wt|A.I. Artificial Intelligence}} (2001, starring [[Haley Joel Osment]] and [[Jude Law]], with [[Robin Williams]], April Grace, [[Paula Malcomson]], [[James W. Jansen]], [[John Prosky]], [[Tim Rigby]], [[Michael Shamus Wiles]], [[Eliza Coleman]], [[Miguel Perez]] and [[Matt Winston]]), {{wt|The United States of Leland}} (2003, with [[Ron Canada]], [[Clyde Kusatsu]], [[Ann Magnuson]], [[Jim Metzler]] and [[Angela Paton]]), ''Fargo'' (2003, with [[Robert Joy]]) and the short film ''The Goldfish'' (with [[Henry Gibson]]), {{wt|Spartan (film)|Spartan}} (2004, with [[Steven Culp]], [[Margot Farley]], [[David Paymer]] and [[Natalia Nogulich]]), ''Sunny & Share Love You'' (2007, with [[Diedrich Bader]]), {{wt|Choke (2008 film)|Choke}} (2008, with [[Joel Grey]] and [[Brad William Henke]]). ''The Last Days of Limbo'' (2008, with [[Ian Abercrombie]]), {{wt|Battle of the Sexes (2017 film)|Battle of the Sexes}} (2017, with Mark Harelik, Wallace Langham, [[Tim Ransom]] and [[Sarah Silverman]]). == Television work == Malloy's first work on television was a starring role on {{wt|Tanner '88}} (with [[Richard Cox]] and [[Wendy Crewson]]). In 1997, Malloy guest-starred on {{wt|The Practice}} (with [[Tony Amendola]]). Also in 1997, Malloy guested on {{wt|TC-16: FBI}} (starring [[Zach Grenier]] with [[Pasha Lychnikoff]] and [[Glenn Morshower]]). In 1999 he worked on {{wt|Spin City}} (starring [[Richard Kind]], Alan Ruck and [[Victoria Dillard]], with [[John Harrington Bland]]). and {{wt|NYPD Blue}} (starring [[Gordon Clapp]] and [[Sharon Lawrence]], with [[Chad Allen]]). In the 21st century, Malloy acted on {{wt|Charmed}} (2001, with [[Michael Bailey Smith]]). On {{wt|Tremors (TV series)|Tremors}}, Malloy worked with [[Melinda Clarke]] (2003). In 2005, Malloy appeared on {{wt|House (TV series)|House}} (starring [[Jennifer Morrison]], with [[John Cho]] and [[Keone Young]]), and {{wt|Without a Trace}} (starring [[Enrique Murciano]] and [[Eric Close]], with [[Marcelo Tubert]] and [[Martin Landau]]). In 2006, Malloy appeared on {{wt|Boston Legal}} with [[René Auberjonois]] and [[William Shatner]] (with [[Ed Begley, Jr.]] and [[Andrew Prine]]), {{wt|The West Wing}} (starring [[Martin Sheen]], with [[Vince Grant]] and [[Scott Klace]]), {{wt|Medium (TV series)|Medium}} (2006, starring [[Jake Weber]], with [[Thomas Jane]], and executive-produced by [[Kelsey Grammer]]), {{wt|Raines}} (with [[Linda Park]]) and {{wt|Numbers (TV series)|Numbers}} (with [[Lisa Vidal]]). Malloy also appeared on {{wt|K-Ville (TV series)|K-Ville}} (starring [[John Carroll Lynch]] with [[Michael Harney]] and Scott Klace), {{wt|Lie to Me}} (2009, with [[Steven Flynn]]), {{wt|Bones (TV series)|Bones}}, (2009, with [[Ellen Geer]], [[Rick Scarry]] and [[Kelvin Yu]]), {{wt|Desperate Housewives}} (2009, starring [[Teri Hatcher]], [[Neal McDonough]] and [[Brenda Strong]]) (with [[John Eric Bentley]]) and {{wt|Hawthorne (TV series)|Hawthorne}} (with [[Bruce French]] and Anne Elizabeth Ramsay) and {{wt|The Mentalist}} (2010, with [[Brian George]]). Malloy has made multiple appearances on {{wt|Law & Order}} from 1993, with [[Carolyn McCormick]]). Also that year with McCormick again was playing a different role. Malloy did gain a recurring role as Roger Pasquese on {{wt|Six Feet Under (TV series)|Six Feet Under}} (starring [[James Cromwell]]). First was "The Black Forest" (with Andrew Prine as well as [[Pat Healy]] and [[Jeff Yagher]]), next were "Bomb Shelter" and "Untitled" (with [[Joanna Cassidy]]) in 2004. Malloy continued in 2005 in "Hold My Hand" and "Time Flies" (with [[Anne Elizabeth Ramsay]]) and with Cromwell only in "All Alone". Malloy was recast in his 1980s role as Deke Connors in ''Tanner on Tanner'' in 2004 with "Dinner at Elaine's" (with Corbin Bernsen) being his only work on the revived series working with another ''Trek'' actor. Malloy was later on {{wt|The Unit}} (2006 & 2007, starring [[Abby Brammell]], former with [[Colby French]], latter directed by [[James Whitmore, Jr.]]). In 2006 Malloy appeared on {{wt|CSI: Crime Scene Investigation}} (starring [[Paul Guilfoyle]], [[Wallace Langham]] and [[Liz Vassey]], with [[Lilyan Chauvin]] and [[Becky Wahlstrom]]). == External links == *{{wikipedia}} *{{imdb|name/nm0540164||external}} {{DEFAULTSORT|Malloy, Matt}} [[de:Matt Malloy]] [[es:Matt Malloy]] [[Category:Performers]] [[Category:ENT performers]] [[Category:Video game performers]]

'''Emilio Borelli''' {{born|3|September|1950}} played the role of [[Frool]] in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 4|fourth season]] episode {{e|Bar Association}}. Borelli is also a theater director.

Borelli starred in the short film ''The Greatest Short Film Ever!!!'', which was written, directed, produced and edited by his "Bar Association" co-star [[Jason Marsden]].

Borelli has guest starred in {{wt|Married... with Children}}, {{wt|Murphy Brown}}, ''Cybill'', {{wt|The Client (TV series)|The Client}} (with [[Derek McGrath]]), {{wt|NYPD Blue}} (1995 & 1997, starring [[Gordon Clapp]] and [[Sharon Lawrence]], latter with [[Dylan Haggerty]] and [[Michael Buchman Silver]]), ''The Tony Danza Show'' (with [[Dean Stockwell]]), {{wt|Just Shoot Me!}} (starring [[Wendie Malick]]), {{wt|Becker (TV series)|Becker}} (with [[Terry Farrell]] and [[Bruce Gray]]), ''That Was Then'' (with [[James Wellington]]), ''The Parkers'', {{wt|Monk (TV series)|Monk}} (2006, starring [[Ted Levine]], with [[Clyde Kusatsu]] and [[Bonita Friedericy]]) and {{wt|Will & Grace}}.

Borelli has also appeared in the motion pictures ''Chameleon'' (with Derek McGrath, [[Tony Amendola]] and [[Wren T. Brown]]), ''Stuart Bliss'' (also with McGrath) and ''Repli-Kate''.

{{real world}} {{sidebar actor |name = Michael Bell |image = Michael Bell.jpg |caption = |birth name = Michael Patrick Bell |birthday = {{d|30|July|1938}} |birthplace = Brooklyn, New York City, New York, USA |deathday = |deathplace = |roles = Actor;
Video game voice actor |characters = [[Zorn]]
[[Borum]]
[[Drofo Awa]] }} '''Michael Patrick Bell''' {{born|30|July|1938}} is an American voice actor and actor from Brooklyn, New York, who portrayed [[Zorn]] in the {{s|TNG}} [[TNG Season 1|first season]] episode {{e|Encounter at Farpoint}}, [[Borum]] in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 2|second season]] episode {{e|The Homecoming}} and [[Drofo Awa]] in {{e|The Maquis, Part II}} later that season. Bell is one of the most prolific voice actors working today, having had roles in hundreds of films and television episodes. Although he has made numerous live-action appearances throughout his career, he is most prominent as a voiceover actor. His large body of voiceover work includes the {{video game}}s ''[[Star Trek: Armada II]]'', ''[[Star Trek: Starfleet Command II: Empires at War]]'', ''[[Star Trek: Deep Space Nine - The Fallen]]'' and ''[[Star Trek: New Worlds]]''. == Film and television voice work == === 1970s === One of Bell's earliest major voice over roles was that of Zan, one of the Wonder Twins, on the various animated ''Super Friends'' cartoons (''The All-New Super Friends Hour'', {{wt|Challenge of the Superfriends}}, {{wt|The World's Greatest SuperFriends}}, and {{wt|Super Friends: The Legendary Super Powers Show}}). On these shows, Bell also provided the vocalizations for the "space monkey," Gleek, and on ''Challenge of the Super Friends'', he voiced the villainous role of The Riddler. This same character was previously played by [[Frank Gorshin]] on the 1960s television series ''Batman'' and was later voiced by [[John Glover]] on ''Batman: The Animated Series'' in the 1990s. During his time on the ''Super Friends'' shows, Bell worked with such voice actors as [[René Auberjonois]], [[Ted Cassidy]], [[Vic Perrin]], [[Mark L. Taylor]] and [[Frank Welker]]. In addition, Bell voiced Mark on {{wt|Speed Buggy}} and Plastic Man on {{wt|The Plastic Man Comedy/Adventure Show}}. He lent his voice to commercials, as well, including Parkay Margarine (where he played the Parkay margarine tub) and Mug Root Beer. === 1980s === Bell was the voice of Grouchy Smurf, Handy Smurf, and Lazy Smurf, as well as the Human, Johan, on [[NBC]]'s {{wt|The Smurfs (1981 TV series)|The Smurfs}}. He worked with many other ''Star Trek'' performers on this show, including [[Hamilton Camp]], [[Barry Gordon]], [[Alan Oppenheimer]], and Frank Welker. During this time, Bell also provided the voices for Duke, Clutch, and several other characters on ''G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero'', the various ''G.I. Joe'' mini-series and {{wt|G.I. Joe: The Movie}} (1987). On {{wt|The Transformers (TV series)|The Transformers}}, Bell voiced no less than eight of the title robotic characters (Bombshell, Brainstorm, First Aid, Gort, Prowl, Scrapper, Sideswipe, and Swoop). Other ''Star Trek'' alumni who supplied voices on this show included [[Roger C. Carmel]], [[Christopher Collins]], [[Walker Edmiston]], [[Paul Eiding]], Alan Oppenheimer, [[Clive Revill]], and Frank Welker. Bell also provided his voice to {{wt|The Transformers: The Movie}}, as did Carmel, Collins, [[B.J. Davis]], Eiding, Revill, Welker, ''Original Series'' regular [[Leonard Nimoy]] and [[Orson Welles]]. Bell's other voice-over roles throughout the 1980s included Bruce Banner and Dr. Octopus on ''The Incredible Hulk'', Lance and Sven on ''Voltron: Defender of the Universe'', and Cyclops in the TV special ''Pryde of the X-Men'' (working with [[Earl Boen]], Alan Oppenheimer and Frank Welker). He voiced characters in animated films, as well, including Grundle in {{wt|My Little Pony: The Movie (1986 film)|My Little Pony: The Movie}} (1986, with [[Catherine Cavadini]]) and Oompy in {{wt|Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland}} (1989, with René Auberjonois, [[Gabriel Damon]] [[Tress MacNeille]] and Alan Oppenheimer). Bell also voiced Lex Luthor in {{wt|Superman (TV series)|Superman}} (1988, sharing the role with [[Sherman Howard]] and [[Clancy Brown]]). === 1990s === During the 1990s, Bell voiced a number of recurring villains on different animated shows. He was Quackerjack on ''Darkwing Duck'' (on which [[Kenneth Mars]] also voiced a recurring villain, namely Tuskernini) and Aziz on ''Aladdin'' (on which [[Jason Alexander]] and [[James Avery]] voiced the most recurring villains, Abis Mal and Harud Hazi Bin), both for Walt Disney Television. He also voiced Ixis Naugus on ''Sonic the Hedgehog'' and Ezekial Rage on ''The Real Adventures of Jonny Quest''. In addition, he was Ferdinand, the scheming, overweight, skateboard-riding dog on {{wt|Tom and Jerry: The Movie}} (1992, with the voices of [[Richard Kind]], [[Henry Gibson]], [[Tony Jay]] and [[David L. Lander]]). Bell is also one of the many ''Star Trek'' alumni to have lent his voice to Disney's animated series, ''Gargoyles''. On this series, Bell voiced the recurring role of Pal Joey, an associate of mob boss Tony Dracon. Among the others who lent their voices to ''Gargoyles'' were [[Diedrich Bader]], [[Clancy Brown]], [[Michael Dorn]], [[Jonathan Frakes]], [[Matt Frewer]], [[Gerrit Graham]], [[Clyde Kusatsu]], [[Kate Mulgrew]], [[Nichelle Nichols]], [[John Rhys-Davies]], [[Salli Elise Richardson]], [[W. Morgan Sheppard]], [[Marina Sirtis]], [[Brent Spiner]], [[David Warner]], Frank Welker and [[Paul Winfield]]. Bell's non-villainous voice-over roles during the 1990s included Opus the penguin on {{wt|A Wish for Wings That Work}} and Captain Grimalken in an episode of ''SWAT Kats: The Radical Squadron''. In the latter, his character's ship is stolen by a villain voiced by ''Next Generation''/''Deep Space Nine'' regular Michael Dorn. Later in the decade, Bell voiced parents Drew Pickles, Chaz Finster and Grandpa Boris Kerpackter on {{dis|Nickelodeon|channel}}'s {{wt|Rugrats}} and {{wt|The Rugrats Movie}} (1998, featuring the voices of [[Whoopi Goldberg]], Tony Jay, [[Andrea Martin]] and [[Iggy Pop]]). He also reprised his role as Lance on {{wt|Voltron: The Third Dimension}}. He also did voice work for an episode of {{wt|The Incredible Hulk (1996 TV series)|The Incredible Hulk}} (with [[Neal McDonough]]). === 2000s === Bell continued voicing Drew Pickles, Chazz Finster and Grandpa Boris on ''Rugrats'' until 2004 and its spin-off series, ''All Grown Up!'', from 2003 through 2008. He also played the first two roles in the films ''Rugrats in Paris'' and ''Rugrats Go Wild'' (with Tony Jay and [[Ethan Phillips]]). Bell parodied his ''Super Friends'' role as Zan in an episode of ''Harvey Birdman: Attorney at Law''. He also voiced Pongo the dalmatian on {{wt|House of Mouse}}. He later played several characters on {{wt|W.I.T.C.H. (TV series)|W.I.T.C.H.}} and he can be heard in the "Brian the Bachelor" episode of [[Seth MacFarlane]]'s ''[[Family Guy]]''. In addition, Bell and Paul Eiding supplied additional voices for {{wt|Cars (film)|Cars}} (2006, with the voices of [[Tom Hanks]], [[Paul Dooley]], [[Jenifer Lewis]], Richard Kind and [[Dave Foley]]). == Video game voice work == Outside of his work in film and television, Bell has supplied his voice to numerous video games since the 1990s. He played various characters in four installments of the ''Baldur's Gate'' video game series, on which he again worked with Earl Boen, Hamilton Camp, Michael Dorn, Alan Oppenheimer and Frank Welker. Bell also worked with [[Brian George]], [[James Horan]], [[Jason Marsden]], [[John Rhys-Davies]], [[Dwight Schultz]] and [[David Warner]] on these games. Bell and [[W. Morgan Sheppard]] voiced Russian soldiers in ''Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty'' (with Earl Boen and Paul Eiding). Bell later voiced The Fear in the sequel, ''Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater'' (with Eiding and [[Richard McGonagle]]). Bell can also be heard on {{wt|Command & Conquer 3: Tiberian Sun}} (2007, with [[Nicholas Worth]]), {{wt|Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2}} (2008, with [[Ray Wise]] and Nicholas Worth), and {{wt|Command & Conquer: Generals – Zero Hour}} (2003, with Brian George, [[Lauren Tom]] and [[James Sie]]). Bell voiced the soul-devouring anti-hero Raziel in three of the ''Legacy of Kain'' video game series, working alongside Tony Jay as the voice of the Elder God. Two of the games also featured the voice of ''Deep Space Nine'' regular René Auberjonois in the role of Janos Audron, an ancient winged vampire resembling an angel, and all of the Franchise's five installments featured [[Simon Templeman]] as the voice of Kain. Bell's many other video game credits include {{wt|Soldier of Fortune II: Double Helix}} (2002, with Earl Boen, [[Rosalind Chao]], [[Lilyan Chauvin]], [[Boris Krutonog]], [[Kenneth Mars]], Alan Oppenheimer and [[Keith Szarabajka]]), ''Diablo II: Lord of Destruction'' (with Paul Eiding), {{wt|Call of Duty (video game)|Call of Duty}} (2003, with [[Greg Ellis]]), and ''Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos'', in addition to many more games with Earl Boen, Alan Oppenheimer and others mentioned above. In the ''[[Star Trek: Starfleet Command|Starfleet Command]]'' series of PC games, Bell has voiced the tutorials for the Romulans, Hydrans and Lyrans, giving each race a distinctive voice. Also appearing in these games were the voices of [[George Takei]], Alan Oppenheimer and [[Cam Clarke]]. == Live-action performances == === Films === Bell appeared in several feature films during the 1950s and 1960s. He had a supporting role in {{wt|Thunder Alley (1967 film)|Thunder Alley}} (1967, with [[Stanley Adams]]). That same year, Bell and [[Sid Haig]] appeared as penthouse lobby guards in {{wt|Point Blank (1967 film)|Point Blank}}, with [[Sharon Acker]], [[James B. Sikking]], [[Michael Strong]], [[Jerry Catron]], [[Felix Silla]], [[Carey Foster]] and [[Chuck Hicks]]. His next film role was a brief appearance in {{wt|Blue (1968 film)|Blue}} (1968, featuring [[Ricardo Montalban]]). Following an uncredited appearance in {{wt|Airport (1970 film)|Airport}} (1970, starring [[Dean Martin]], with set decoration by [[Mickey S. Michaels]]), Bell had a role in {{wt|Brother John (film)|Brother John}} (1971, with [[Paul Winfield]]). This film was directed by [[James Goldstone]], whom Bell first worked with on the 1970 TV movie ''A Clear and Present Danger'' (co-starring Sharon Acker and [[Jeff Corey]]) and with whom he reunited several years later for {{wt|Rollercoaster (1977 film)|Rollercoaster}} (1977). Bell has only appeared in three films since ''Rollercoaster''. The first was [[Robert Scheerer]]'s {{wt|How to Beat the High Cost of Living}} (1980, co-starring [[Byron Morrow]]). He later appeared in {{wt|C.H.U.D. II: Bud the Chud}} (1989) with [[Larry Cedar]], [[Gerrit Graham]] and [[Robert Symonds]]. He later played Marvis in {{wt|A Thin Line Between Love and Hate}} (1996). === Television === During the 1960s, Bell guest-starred on several hit TV programs, including {{wt|Gomer Pyle – USMC}}, {{wt|Get Smart}}, {{wt|The Monkees (TV series)|The Monkees}}, and ''The Big Valley''. He was seen in the pilot episode of NBC's ''Then Came Bronson'', as well, and appeared on {{wt|Here Come the Brides}} (1967, starring [[Robert Brown]], [[David Soul]] and [[Mark Lenard]]). He also worked with director [[Alexander Singer]] on episodes of {{wt|The Monkees (TV series)|The Monkees}} (with [[Victor Tayback]]) and [[Desilu]]'s ''[[Mission: Impossible]]'' (with [[Robert Ellenstein]]). Between 1970 and 1974, Bell appeared in six episodes of NBC's {{wt|Ironside (1967 TV series)|Ironside}}, each time playing a different character. [[Barbara Anderson]] was a regular on this series for Bell's first two episodes. His very first episode, "Little Jerry Jessup," guest-starred {{S|TOS}} star [[William Shatner]] as well as fellow ''Deep Space Nine'' guest actor [[Kenneth Tobey]]. ''Star Trek'' alumni he worked with on subsequent episodes this show included performers [[Vince Howard]], [[Gene Lyons]], [[Phillip Pine]] and directors [[Don McDougall]] and Robert Scheerer. Bell again worked with Don McDougall on {{wt|Mannix}} (1972, with [[Steve Ihnat]], [[Julie Parrish]] and [[Norman Stuart]]. McDougall also directed Bell on the 1972 ABC Movie of the Week ''The Heist'', which co-starred [[Arthur Batanides]] and [[Paul Sorensen]]. Bell's other TV appearances during the early 1970s included two additional episodes of ''Mannix'' (working with [[Barry Atwater]], [[Paul Carr]], [[Walker Edmiston]], [[Rosemary Forsyth]], [[Chuck Hicks]], [[Frank Orsatti]], [[Jay Robinson]] and Kenneth Tobey), an episode of {{wt|Cannon (TV series)|Cannon}} with [[Richard Kiley]], a pair of crossover episodes between ''Cannon'' and {{wt|Barnaby Jones}} (1975, starring [[Lee Meriwether]], with Sharon Acker and [[George D. Wallace]]), and several episodes of ''Petrocelli'' (starring [[Susan Howard]] and [[David Huddleston]]). Between 1975 and 1986, Bell appeared on such shows as ''The Streets of San Francisco'' (with Paul Carr, [[Sherry Jackson]], [[Charles Napier]] and Phillip Pine), {{wt|Charlie's Angels}} (starring [[Kate Jackson]], including an episode with [[Ed Lauter]]), {{wt|The Rockford Files}} (1976 & 1977, latter directed by [[Reza Badiyi]] and featuring Ed Lauter and [[Bill Quinn]]), ''CHiPs'' (starring [[Robert Pine]]), {{wt|Fame (1982 TV series)|Fame}}, with director Robert Scheerer), {{wt|Remington Steele}} (starring [[Pierce Brosnan]], with [[Camille Saviola]]), and {{wt|Scarecrow and Mrs. King}} (1986, starring Kate Jackson, with [[William Schallert]]). He has also been seen on {{wt|M*A*S*H (TV series)|M*A*S*H}}, {{wt|Benson (TV series)|Benson}}, and ''Three's Comedy''. Perhaps his most notable live-action television role was that of recurring character Les Crowley in four episodes of {{wt|Dallas (TV series)|Dallas}} airing in late 1980 and early 1981. Among the ''Star Trek'' performers he worked with on this series were [[Barbara Babcock]], [[Mary Crosby]], [[Ted Gehring]], [[Richard Herd]], Susan Howard, [[Leigh J. McCloskey]], [[William Smithers]], Paul Sorensen and [[Morgan Woodward]]. Bell made a return visit to the series in 1991, albeit as a different character. Bell has not appeared in a live-action TV project since his last appearance on ''Deep Space Nine'' in 1994. == ''Star Trek'' appearances == File:Zorn.jpg|[[Zorn]]

[[Joran Belar]] |image = Tieran.jpg |caption = ... as Tieran }} '''Leigh McCloskey''' {{born|21|June|1955}} is an actor, artist and author who played [[Tieran]] in the {{s|VOY}} [[VOY Season 3|third season]] episode {{e|Warlord}} and an [[Illusory people#Belar, Joran|illusory]] [[Joran Belar]] in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 7|seventh season]] episode {{e|Field of Fire}}. Born in Los Angeles, California, McCloskey attended the Juilliard School in New York where his roommate was fellow ''[[Star Trek]]'' guest actor [[Kelsey Grammer]]. McCloskey started his acting career in the 1970s with appearances in {{wt|Phyllis (TV series)|Phyllis}} (1975), ''The Streets of San Francisco'' (1975, with [[Eric Server]]), {{wt|Rich Man, Poor Man (miniseries)|Rich Man, Poor Man}} (1976, with [[Lawrence Pressman]], [[Kim Darby]] and [[Fionnula Flanagan]] and executive produced by [[Harve Bennett]]), {{wt|Hawaii Five-O (1968 TV series)|Hawaii Five-O}} (1977, starring [[Jack Lord]]), ''The Paper Chase'' (1979, with [[Charles Hallahan]] and [[Tony Plana]]), and ''Buck Rogers in the 25th Century'' (1979, with [[Tim O'Connor]], [[Felix Silla]] and [[Patty Maloney]]). He played the lead role in {{wt|Executive Suite (TV series)|Executive Suite}} (1976-77, starring [[Mitchell Ryan]] and [[Sharon Acker]], with [[Byron Morrow]], [[Madlyn Rhue]], [[William Smithers]] and [[Richard Cox]]) and ''Married: The First Year'' (1979, with [[Claudette Nevins]] and [[K Callan]]). Film work in the 1970s include {{wt|Dawn: Portrait of a Teenage Runaway}} (1976, with [[William Schallert]] and [[Paul Sorensen]]), {{wt|Alexander: The Other Side of Dawn}} (1977, with [[Jonathan Banks]]), {{wt|The Bermuda Depths}} (1978), and ''Doctor's Private Lives'' (1978, with [[Barbara Anderson]] and [[Kim Hamilton]]). Between 1980 and 1988, he played Mitch Cooper in 46 episodes of {{wt|Dallas (TV series)|Dallas}} and worked with [[Susan Howard]], [[Joshua Harris]], William Smithers, [[John Beck]], [[Morgan Woodward]] and [[Mary Crosby]]. Between 1988 and 1990 he first portrayed Dr. Zach Kelton and later Ethan Asher for 246 episodes in {{wt|Santa Barbara (TV series)|Santa Barbara}}. Among his numerous guest roles in the 1980s are episodes of {{wt|Hart to Hart}} (1981, with [[Ron Glass]]), {{wt|The Fall Guy}} (1983), ''Mike Hammer'' (1984, with [[Nick Dimitri]]), {{wt|Fantasy Island}} (1984, starring [[Ricardo Montalban]]), ''The Love Boat'' (1983-85, with [[Jim Lau]] and [[Teri Hatcher]]), {{wt|Murder, She Wrote}} (1986, with [[Michael Horton]]), {{wt|Hotel (American TV series)|Hotel}} (1983, 1985 & 1986, with [[Michael Spound]], [[Michelle Phillips]], [[Leigh Taylor-Young]], [[Alan Oppenheimer]] and [[Nehemiah Persoff]]), and ''The Bronx Zoo'' (1988). Film work in the 1980s include {{wt|Fraternity Vacation}} (1985, with [[Matt McCoy]] and [[Charles Rocket]]), {{wt|Just One of the Guys}} (1985, with [[Clayton Rohner]], [[Kenneth Tigar]], [[Stuart Charno]] and [[Katy Boyer]]), {{wt|Hamburger: The Motion Picture}} (1986, with [[Jack Blessing]], [[Bob Minor]] and [[Tony Epper]]), and ''Dirty Laundry'' (1987, with [[Nicholas Worth]] and [[Herta Ware]]), and the action thriller ''Double Revenge'' (1988, with [[Vinny Argiro]] and [[Matt Roe]]). McCloskey originated the role of Dr. Kurt Costner in {{wt|The Young and the Restless}} when he appeared in three episodes in 1996/1997. In 2013 he reprised this role and appeared in fifteen more episodes. '''Christopher Neiman''' {{born|28|June|1966}} is the actor who played [[Yeggie]] in the {{s|VOY}} [[VOY Season 7|seventh season]] episode {{e|Inside Man}}. 

== Career ==
=== Television ===
Neiman made his television debut in a 1998 episode of ''[[The X-Files]]'' directed by [[Kim Manners]], starring [[Gillian Anderson]], with [[Wendie Malick]], [[George Murdock]], [[Wayne Thomas Yorke]], [[Cazimir Milostan]] and [[Benito Martinez]]. The following year, he made an appearances on {{wt|3rd Rock from the Sun}} (with his "Inside Man" co-star, [[Richard McGonagle]]), [[UPN]]'s {{wt|G vs E}} (1999, starring [[Clayton Rohner]]), and [[J.J. Abrams]]'s {{wt|Felicity (TV series)|Felicity}} (1999, starring [[Keri Russell]], with [[Amanda Foreman]]).

From 1999 through 2001, Neiman a recurring role as Attorney Barry Mathers on {{wt|Ally McBeal}}. During his time on this show, Neiman worked with such performers as [[Albert Hall]], [[Famke Janssen]], [[Kevin Rahm]], [[Jack Shearer]] and [[William Windom]]. Neiman also appeared in the first episode of {{wt|Boston Public}}. In 2007, he appeared with [[René Auberjonois]] in {{wt|Boston Legal}}, which also starred [[William Shatner]]. 

In addition, Neiman has been seen on shows such as {{wt|The West Wing}} (starring [[Martin Sheen]], with [[John Billingsley]]), [[Whoopi Goldberg]]'s {{wt|Strong Medicine}} (starring [[Jenifer Lewis]]), {{wt|Everwood}} (with [[Stephanie Niznik]]), {{wt|JAG (TV series)|JAG}} (with Richard McGonagle, in an episode also featuring [[Scott Lawrence]], [[Zoe McLellan]], [[William Sadler]], [[Dean Stockwell]], and [[Ray Wise]]), {{wt|Six Feet Under (TV series)|Six Feet Under}} (co-starring [[Abby Brammell]], [[Joanna Cassidy]], [[Rosalind Chao]] and [[James Cromwell]]), and [[Bryan Fuller]]'s ''Pushing Daisies''. He also had a two-episode recurring role on ''The Guardian'' (with [[Erich Anderson]], [[Tracy Middendorf]], [[Jeff Ricketts]] and [[Raphael Sbarge]]) and, in 2004, played the recurring role of Sigmund on {{wt|Charmed}} (including an episode with [[Annie Wersching]]).

=== Films ===
Neiman had roles in two films released in 1999: ''Enemy Action'' (co-starring [[Henry Darrow]], [[Richard Lynch]] and [[Carel Struycken]]) and ''Restraining Order'' (with [[Ed McCready]], [[Natalia Nogulich]], [[Dean Stockwell]] and [[Spice Williams]]). He also had a role in {{wt|Hellraiser: Inferno}}, which was released directly to home video in 2000. [[Michael Shamus Wiles]] appeared in this film, as well.

In 2001, he appeared in {{wt|Surviving Gilligan's Island}} as Network Executive # 2, alongside fellow Star Trek alumni [[Aaron Lustig]], [[Steve Vinovich]], [[Michael Wiseman]], [[Ray Buktenica]], and [[Jim Jansen]].

In 2002, Neiman was seen as {{wt|Hogan's Heroes}} actor {{w|Robert Clary}} in {{wt|Auto Focus}}, which co-starred [[Nikita Ager]], [[Ed Begley, Jr.]], [[Michael McKean]] and [[Don McManus]]. He also appeared in {{wt|Simone (2002 film)|Simone}} that same year, starring [[Winona Ryder]] with [[Rebecca Romijn]]. He later appeared in {{wt|The Longest Yard (2005 film)|The Longest Yard}} (2005, starring James Cromwell and [[Ed Lauter]]) and in [[Corbin Bernsen]]'s 2005 comedy ''Carpool Guy''.

=== Video games ===
In addition to his film and TV work, Neiman also lent his voice to two installments in the ''[[w:c:lands-of-lore:Lands of Lore Wiki|Lands of Lore]]'' video game series. The first was {{wt|Lands of Lore: Guardians of Destiny}} in 1997, which also featured the voices of [[Clancy Brown]], [[Sherman Howard]], [[Julie Newmar]] and [[Vincent Schiavelli]]. The second, 1999's {{wt|Lands of Lore III}}, also featured the voice of Clancy Brown, as well as [[Darleen Carr]].

'''Michael William Rivkin''' {{born|27|April|1967}} is the actor who portrayed [[DaiMon]] [[Nunk]] in the {{s|VOY}} [[VOY Season 7|seventh season]] episode {{e|Inside Man}}. He is probably best known for his role as the man with Harvey, the dog in {{wt|Men in Black II}} (2002, with [[Rosario Dawson]], [[Jack Kehler]], [[Michael Bailey Smith]], [[Mary Stein]], [[Doug Jones]], [[Kevin Grevioux]], [[Derek Mears]], [[Gene LeBell]], [[Shannon Watson]] and [[Bart Mixon]]) and as a member of the comedy/rap duo {{w|Supafloss}}.

Rivkin started his acting career in the late '80s and appeared in films such as the thriller ''Freeway Maniac'' (1989, with [[Donald Hotton]] and [[Gary Wayton]]), the comedy ''The Shot'' (1996, with Jack Kehler and [[Natalia Nogulich]]), {{wt|The Cable Guy}} (1996, with [[Andy Dick]], [[Tommy Hinkley]], [[Lloyd Kino]], [[Charles Napier]], [[Christopher Michael]], [[David Bowe]], and [[Sean Whalen]]), {{wt|Dead Man on Campus}} (1998), {{wt|Desperate but Not Serious}} (1999, with [[Patton Oswalt]], [[Patti Tippo]], [[John Fleck]], [[Herta Ware]], and [[Joy Kilpatrick]]), and {{wt|Cradle Will Rock}} (1999, with [[Lee Arenberg]], [[Harris Yulin]], [[Paul Giamatti]], [[Tony Amendola]] and Patti Tippo).

He also appeared in television series, including {{wt|Seinfeld}} (1994, with [[Jason Alexander]] and [[Thomas Dekker]]), ''Grace Under Fire'' (1995, with [[Jon Paul Steuer]] and [[Paul Dooley]]), {{wt|Jenny (TV series)|Jenny}} (1997, along [[Alex Nevil]], [[Richard Libertini]] and [[Rebecca McFarland]]), {{wt|Judging Amy}} (1999, with [[Lawrence Pressman]] and [[Michael Buchman Silver]]), and {{wt|Charmed}} (2000, with [[J.P. Romano]]).

His ''Voyager'' role was followed by the science fiction films ''The Zeros'' (2001, with [[Jennifer Morrison]]) and {{wt|The Void (2001 film)|The Void}} (2001, with [[Malcolm McDowell]]), {{wt|ER (TV series)|ER}} (2005, with [[Scott Grimes]], [[Leland Orser]] and [[Lily Mariye]]), the short science fiction film ''The Futurist'' (2005), and two appearances in {{wt|Kitchen Confidential (TV series)|Kitchen Confidential}} (2005, with [[John Cho]] and [[Clement von Franckenstein]]; 2006, with John Cho, [[Frank Langella]] and [[Concetta Tomei]]).

Rivkin later played a supporting role in {{wt|Tenacious D in The Pick of Destiny}} (2006, with [[Paul F. Tompkins]], [[Stephanie Erb]] and [[Bevin Kaye]]), had a guest role in {{wt|House (TV series)|House}} (2007, with Jennifer Morrison), and {{wt|Barry Munday}} (2008, with Malcolm McDowell, [[Christopher McDonald]], [[Michael Durrell]], [[Matt Winston]] and [[Missi Pyle]]).
